***Apology for Smectymnuus***, or *An Apology for a Pamphlet*, was published by [John Milton](/wiki/John_Milton "John Milton") in April 1642. It was the final of his [antiprelatical tracts](/wiki/Milton%27s_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts") which criticize the structure of the [Church of England](/wiki/Church_of_England "Church of England").

Background
----------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background")]

The *[Apology](/wiki/Apologetics "Apologetics")* was published in April 1642 as *An Apology against a Pamphlet Called a Modest Confutation of the Animadversions upon the Remonstrant against Smectymnvvs* and is [his final antiprelatical tract](/wiki/Milton%27s_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts"). The tract was written as a response to a refutation by Bishop [Joseph Hall](/wiki/Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)").[[1]](#cite_note-1)

Tract
-----

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Tract")]

Milton argues that the defense of truth makes one vulnerable to personal attacks and emphasizes that role of personal integrity, especially his own:[[2]](#cite_note-2) "as a member incorporate into that truth whereof I was perswaded".[[3]](#cite_note-3) Milton defends his own integrity when he later writes:[[4]](#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) "that indeed according to art is most eloquent, which returns and approaches neerest to nature from whence it came; and they expresse nature best, who in their lives least wander from her safe leading, which may be call'd regenerate reason".[[5]](#cite_note-5) This idea is expanded further when he says:

> he who would not be frustrated of his hope to write well hereafter in laudable things, ought him selfe to bee a true Poem, that is, a composition, and patterne of the best and honourable things; not presuming to sing high praises of heroick men, or famous Cities, unlesse he have in himselfe the experience and the practice of all that which is praise-worthy.[[6]](#cite_note-6)

Themes
------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Themes")]

The *Apology*, like many of Milton's other tracts, praises Parliament and emphasizes that they are reformers and the basis of the country.[[7]](#cite_note-7) The tract also connects truth of words with the individual's character.[[4]](#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) Paul Stevens emphasizes that the tract reflects how "Milton's self is produced in the process of writing" and that his self is put through "a series of culturally approved *laterall* transformations".[[8]](#cite_note-8) In particular, Elizabeth Wheeler points out that the tract contains "Milton's understanding of [Aristotle](/wiki/Aristotle "Aristotle")'s definition of man as a political animal. Heroism lies in the risk of changing and being changed in verbal exchange."[[9]](#cite_note-9)

The *Apology*, like many of Milton's other tracts, praises Parliament and emphasizes that they are reformers and the basis of the country.[[7]](#cite_note-7) The tract also connects truth of words with the individual's character.[[4]](#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) Paul Stevens emphasizes that the tract reflects how "Milton's self is produced in the process of writing" and that his self is put through "a series of culturally approved *laterall* transformations".[[8]](#cite_note-8) In particular, Elizabeth Wheeler points out that the tract contains "Milton's understanding of [Aristotle](/wiki/Aristotle "Aristotle")'s definition of man as a political animal. Heroism lies in the risk of changing and being changed in verbal exchange."[[9]](#cite_note-9)

***Apology for Smectymnuus***, or *An Apology for a Pamphlet*, was published by [John Milton](/wiki/John_Milton "John Milton") in April 1642. It was the final of his [antiprelatical tracts](/wiki/Milton%27s_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts") which criticize the structure of the [Church of England](/wiki/Church_of_England "Church of England").

Background
----------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background")]

The *[Apology](/wiki/Apologetics "Apologetics")* was published in April 1642 as *An Apology against a Pamphlet Called a Modest Confutation of the Animadversions upon the Remonstrant against Smectymnvvs* and is [his final antiprelatical tract](/wiki/Milton%27s_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts"). The tract was written as a response to a refutation by Bishop [Joseph Hall](/wiki/Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)").[[1]](#cite_note-1)

Tract
-----

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Tract")]

Milton argues that the defense of truth makes one vulnerable to personal attacks and emphasizes that role of personal integrity, especially his own:[[2]](#cite_note-2) "as a member incorporate into that truth whereof I was perswaded".[[3]](#cite_note-3) Milton defends his own integrity when he later writes:[[4]](#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) "that indeed according to art is most eloquent, which returns and approaches neerest to nature from whence it came; and they expresse nature best, who in their lives least wander from her safe leading, which may be call'd regenerate reason".[[5]](#cite_note-5) This idea is expanded further when he says:

> he who would not be frustrated of his hope to write well hereafter in laudable things, ought him selfe to bee a true Poem, that is, a composition, and patterne of the best and honourable things; not presuming to sing high praises of heroick men, or famous Cities, unlesse he have in himselfe the experience and the practice of all that which is praise-worthy.[[6]](#cite_note-6)

Themes
------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Themes")]

The *Apology*, like many of Milton's other tracts, praises Parliament and emphasizes that they are reformers and the basis of the country.[[7]](#cite_note-7) The tract also connects truth of words with the individual's character.[[4]](#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) Paul Stevens emphasizes that the tract reflects how "Milton's self is produced in the process of writing" and that his self is put through "a series of culturally approved *laterall* transformations".[[8]](#cite_note-8) In particular, Elizabeth Wheeler points out that the tract contains "Milton's understanding of [Aristotle](/wiki/Aristotle "Aristotle")'s definition of man as a political animal. Heroism lies in the risk of changing and being changed in verbal exchange."[[9]](#cite_note-9)

***Apology for Smectymnuus***, or *An Apology for a Pamphlet*, was published by [John Milton](/wiki/John_Milton "John Milton") in April 1642. It was the final of his [antiprelatical tracts](/wiki/Milton%27s_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts") which criticize the structure of the [Church of England](/wiki/Church_of_England "Church of England").

Background
----------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background")]

The *[Apology](/wiki/Apologetics "Apologetics")* was published in April 1642 as *An Apology against a Pamphlet Called a Modest Confutation of the Animadversions upon the Remonstrant against Smectymnvvs* and is [his final antiprelatical tract](/wiki/Milton%27s_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts"). The tract was written as a response to a refutation by Bishop [Joseph Hall](/wiki/Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)").[[1]](#cite_note-1)

Tract
-----

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Tract")]

Milton argues that the defense of truth makes one vulnerable to personal attacks and emphasizes that role of personal integrity, especially his own:[[2]](#cite_note-2) "as a member incorporate into that truth whereof I was perswaded".[[3]](#cite_note-3) Milton defends his own integrity when he later writes:[[4]](#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) "that indeed according to art is most eloquent, which returns and approaches neerest to nature from whence it came; and they expresse nature best, who in their lives least wander from her safe leading, which may be call'd regenerate reason".[[5]](#cite_note-5) This idea is expanded further when he says:

> he who would not be frustrated of his hope to write well hereafter in laudable things, ought him selfe to bee a true Poem, that is, a composition, and patterne of the best and honourable things; not presuming to sing high praises of heroick men, or famous Cities, unlesse he have in himselfe the experience and the practice of all that which is praise-worthy.[[6]](#cite_note-6)

Themes
------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Themes")]

The *Apology*, like many of Milton's other tracts, praises Parliament and emphasizes that they are reformers and the basis of the country.[[7]](#cite_note-7) The tract also connects truth of words with the individual's character.[[4]](#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) Paul Stevens emphasizes that the tract reflects how "Milton's self is produced in the process of writing" and that his self is put through "a series of culturally approved *laterall* transformations".[[8]](#cite_note-8) In particular, Elizabeth Wheeler points out that the tract contains "Milton's understanding of [Aristotle](/wiki/Aristotle "Aristotle")'s definition of man as a political animal. Heroism lies in the risk of changing and being changed in verbal exchange."[[9]](#cite_note-9)

It was the final of his [antiprelatical tracts](/wiki/Milton%27s_antiprelatical_tracts \"Milton\\'s antiprelatical tracts\") which criticize the structure of the [Church of England](/wiki/Church_of_England \"Church of England\").\\n\\nBackground\\n----------\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=1 \"Edit section: Background\")]\\n\\nThe *[Apology](/wiki/Apologetics \"Apologetics\")* was published in April 1642 as *An Apology against a Pamphlet Called a Modest Confutation of the Animadversions upon the Remonstrant against Smectymnvvs* and is [his final antiprelatical tract](/wiki/Milton%27s_antiprelatical_tracts \"Milton\\'s antiprelatical tracts\"). The tract was written as a response to a refutation by Bishop [Joseph Hall](/wiki/Joseph_Hall_(bishop) \"Joseph Hall (bishop)\").[[1]](#cite_note-1)\\n\\nTract\\n-----\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=2 \"Edit section: Tract\")]\\n\\nMilton argues that the defense of truth makes one vulnerable to personal attacks and emphasizes that role of personal integrity, especially his own:[[2]](#cite_note-2) \"as a member incorporate into that truth whereof I was perswaded\".[[3]](#cite_note-3) Milton defends his own integrity when he later writes:[[4]](#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) \"that indeed according to art is most eloquent, which returns and approaches neerest to nature from whence it came; and they expresse nature best, who in their lives least wander from her safe leading, which may be call\\'d regenerate reason\".[[5]](#cite_note-5) This idea is expanded further when he says:\\n\\n> he who would not be frustrated of his hope to write well hereafter in laudable things, ought him selfe to bee a true Poem, that is, a composition, and patterne of the best and honourable things; From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Group of clergy active in 1641 England

**Smectymnuus** was the *[nom de plume](/wiki/Pen_name "Pen name")* of a group of [Puritan](/wiki/Puritan "Puritan") clergymen active in [England](/wiki/England "England") in 1641 during the reign of [Charles I](/wiki/Charles_I_of_England,_Scotland,_and_Ireland "Charles I of England, Scotland, and Ireland"). It comprised four leading English churchmen, and one Scottish minister ([Thomas Young](/wiki/Thomas_Young_(1587-1655) "Thomas Young (1587-1655)")). They went on to provide leadership for the anti-episcopal forces in the [Church of England](/wiki/Church_of_England "Church of England"), continuing into the [Westminster Assembly](/wiki/Westminster_Assembly "Westminster Assembly"), where they also opposed the Independent movement.

The name is an acronym derived from the initials of the five authors: [Stephen Marshall](/wiki/Stephen_Marshall_(English_clergyman) "Stephen Marshall (English clergyman)"), [Edmund Calamy](/wiki/Edmund_Calamy_the_Elder "Edmund Calamy the Elder"), Thomas Young, [Matthew Newcomen](/wiki/Matthew_Newcomen "Matthew Newcomen"), and [William Spurstow](/wiki/William_Spurstow "William Spurstow"). ***Apology for Smectymnuus***, or *An Apology for a Pamphlet*, was published by [John Milton](/wiki/John_Milton "John Milton") in April 1642. It was the final of his [antiprelatical tracts](/wiki/Milton%27s_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts") which criticize the structure of the [Church of England](/wiki/Church_of_England "Church of England").

Background
----------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background")]

The *[Apology](/wiki/Apologetics "Apologetics")* was published in April 1642 as *An Apology against a Pamphlet Called a Modest Confutation of the Animadversions upon the Remonstrant against Smectymnvvs* and is [his final antiprelatical tract](/wiki/Milton%27s_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts"). The tract was written as a response to a refutation by Bishop [Joseph Hall](/wiki/Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)").[[1]](#cite_note-1)

Tract
-----

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Tract")]

Milton argues that the defense of truth makes one vulnerable to personal attacks and emphasizes that role of personal integrity, especially his own:[[2]](#cite_note-2) "as a member incorporate into that truth whereof I was perswaded".[[3]](#cite_note-3) Milton defends his own integrity when he later writes:[[4]](#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) "that indeed according to art is most eloquent, which returns and approaches neerest to nature from whence it came; and they expresse nature best, who in their lives least wander from her safe leading, which may be call'd regenerate reason".[[5]](#cite_note-5) This idea is expanded further when he says:

> he who would not be frustrated of his hope to write well hereafter in laudable things, ought him selfe to bee a true Poem, that is, a composition, and patterne of the best and honourable things; not presuming to sing high praises of heroick men, or famous Cities, unlesse he have in himselfe the experience and the practice of all that which is praise-worthy.[[6]](#cite_note-6)

Themes
------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Themes")]

The *Apology*, like many of Milton's other tracts, praises Parliament and emphasizes that they are reformers and the basis of the country.[[7]](#cite_note-7) The tract also connects truth of words with the individual's character.[[4]](#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) Paul Stevens emphasizes that the tract reflects how "Milton's self is produced in the process of writing" and that his self is put through "a series of culturally approved *laterall* transformations".[[8]](#cite_note-8) In particular, Elizabeth Wheeler points out that the tract contains "Milton's understanding of [Aristotle](/wiki/Aristotle "Aristotle")'s definition of man as a political animal. Heroism lies in the risk of changing and being changed in verbal exchange."[[9]](#cite_note-9)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Group of clergy active in 1641 England

**Smectymnuus** was the *[nom de plume](/wiki/Pen_name "Pen name")* of a group of [Puritan](/wiki/Puritan "Puritan") clergymen active in [England](/wiki/England "England") in 1641 during the reign of [Charles I](/wiki/Charles_I_of_England,_Scotland,_and_Ireland "Charles I of England, Scotland, and Ireland"). It comprised four leading English churchmen, and one Scottish minister ([Thomas Young](/wiki/Thomas_Young_(1587-1655) "Thomas Young (1587-1655)")). They went on to provide leadership for the anti-episcopal forces in the [Church of England](/wiki/Church_of_England "Church of England"), continuing into the [Westminster Assembly](/wiki/Westminster_Assembly "Westminster Assembly"), where they also opposed the Independent movement.

The name is an acronym derived from the initials of the five authors: [Stephen Marshall](/wiki/Stephen_Marshall_(English_clergyman) "Stephen Marshall (English clergyman)"), [Edmund Calamy](/wiki/Edmund_Calamy_the_Elder "Edmund Calamy the Elder"), Thomas Young, [Matthew Newcomen](/wiki/Matthew_Newcomen "Matthew Newcomen"), and [William Spurstow](/wiki/William_Spurstow "William Spurstow"). Their first pamphlet, *An Answer to a booke entituled, An Humble Remonstrance. In Which, the Original of Liturgy and Episcopacy is discussed*, appeared in March 1641. The pamphlet was written in response to [Joseph Hall's](/wiki/Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)") *An Humble Remonstrance to the High Court of Parliament*. It is thought that [John Milton](/wiki/John_Milton "John Milton") wrote the postscript for Smectymnuus's reply.[[1]](#cite_note-1)

This response provoked Hall to write another reply: *A Defence of the Humble Remonstrance, against the Frivolous and false Expectations of Smectymnuus*. Smectymnuus answered Hall again with their *A Vindication of the Answer to the Humble Remonstrance, from the Unjust Imputations of Frivolousnesse and Falsehood*.

Milton also published two tracts defending the Smectymnuus group from Hall: *[Animadversions upon The Remonstrants Defence Against Smectymnvvs](/wiki/Animadversions "Animadversions")* (1641) and *[Apology for Smectymnuus](/wiki/Apology_for_Smectymnuus "Apology for Smectymnuus")* (1642).[[2]](#cite_note-2) Thomas Young was a former tutor and close friend to Milton.[[3]](#cite_note-3)

***Apology for Smectymnuus***, or *An Apology for a Pamphlet*, was published by [John Milton](/wiki/John_Milton "John Milton") in April 1642. It was the final of his [antiprelatical tracts](/wiki/Milton%27s_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts") which criticize the structure of the [Church of England](/wiki/Church_of_England "Church of England").

Background
----------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background")]

The *[Apology](/wiki/Apologetics "Apologetics")* was published in April 1642 as *An Apology against a Pamphlet Called a Modest Confutation of the Animadversions upon the Remonstrant against Smectymnvvs* and is [his final antiprelatical tract](/wiki/Milton%27s_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts"). The tract was written as a response to a refutation by Bishop [Joseph Hall](/wiki/Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)").[[1]](#cite_note-1)

Tract
-----

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Tract")]

Milton argues that the defense of truth makes one vulnerable to personal attacks and emphasizes that role of personal integrity, especially his own:[[2]](#cite_note-2) "as a member incorporate into that truth whereof I was perswaded".[[3]](#cite_note-3) Milton defends his own integrity when he later writes:[[4]](#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) "that indeed according to art is most eloquent, which returns and approaches neerest to nature from whence it came; and they expresse nature best, who in their lives least wander from her safe leading, which may be call'd regenerate reason".[[5]](#cite_note-5) This idea is expanded further when he says:

> he who would not be frustrated of his hope to write well hereafter in laudable things, ought him selfe to bee a true Poem, that is, a composition, and patterne of the best and honourable things; not presuming to sing high praises of heroick men, or famous Cities, unlesse he have in himselfe the experience and the practice of all that which is praise-worthy.[[6]](#cite_note-6)

Themes
------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Themes")]

The *Apology*, like many of Milton's other tracts, praises Parliament and emphasizes that they are reformers and the basis of the country.[[7]](#cite_note-7) The tract also connects truth of words with the individual's character.[[4]](#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) Paul Stevens emphasizes that the tract reflects how "Milton's self is produced in the process of writing" and that his self is put through "a series of culturally approved *laterall* transformations".[[8]](#cite_note-8) In particular, Elizabeth Wheeler points out that the tract contains "Milton's understanding of [Aristotle](/wiki/Aristotle "Aristotle")'s definition of man as a political animal. Heroism lies in the risk of changing and being changed in verbal exchange."[[9]](#cite_note-9)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Group of clergy active in 1641 England

**Smectymnuus** was the *[nom de plume](/wiki/Pen_name "Pen name")* of a group of [Puritan](/wiki/Puritan "Puritan") clergymen active in [England](/wiki/England "England") in 1641 during the reign of [Charles I](/wiki/Charles_I_of_England,_Scotland,_and_Ireland "Charles I of England, Scotland, and Ireland"). It comprised four leading English churchmen, and one Scottish minister ([Thomas Young](/wiki/Thomas_Young_(1587-1655) "Thomas Young (1587-1655)")). They went on to provide leadership for the anti-episcopal forces in the [Church of England](/wiki/Church_of_England "Church of England"), continuing into the [Westminster Assembly](/wiki/Westminster_Assembly "Westminster Assembly"), where they also opposed the Independent movement.

The name is an acronym derived from the initials of the five authors: [Stephen Marshall](/wiki/Stephen_Marshall_(English_clergyman) "Stephen Marshall (English clergyman)"), [Edmund Calamy](/wiki/Edmund_Calamy_the_Elder "Edmund Calamy the Elder"), Thomas Young, [Matthew Newcomen](/wiki/Matthew_Newcomen "Matthew Newcomen"), and [William Spurstow](/wiki/William_Spurstow "William Spurstow"). Their first pamphlet, *An Answer to a booke entituled, An Humble Remonstrance. In Which, the Original of Liturgy and Episcopacy is discussed*, appeared in March 1641. The pamphlet was written in response to [Joseph Hall's](/wiki/Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)") *An Humble Remonstrance to the High Court of Parliament*. It is thought that [John Milton](/wiki/John_Milton "John Milton") wrote the postscript for Smectymnuus's reply.[[1]](#cite_note-1)

This response provoked Hall to write another reply: *A Defence of the Humble Remonstrance, against the Frivolous and false Expectations of Smectymnuus*. Smectymnuus answered Hall again with their *A Vindication of the Answer to the Humble Remonstrance, from the Unjust Imputations of Frivolousnesse and Falsehood*.

Milton also published two tracts defending the Smectymnuus group from Hall: *[Animadversions upon The Remonstrants Defence Against Smectymnvvs](/wiki/Animadversions "Animadversions")* (1641) and *[Apology for Smectymnuus](/wiki/Apology_for_Smectymnuus "Apology for Smectymnuus")* (1642).[[2]](#cite_note-2) Thomas Young was a former tutor and close friend to Milton.[[3]](#cite_note-3)

It was the final of his [antiprelatical tracts](/wiki/Milton%27s_antiprelatical_tracts \"Milton\\'s antiprelatical tracts\") which criticize the structure of the [Church of England](/wiki/Church_of_England \"Church of England\").\\n\\nBackground\\n----------\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=1 \"Edit section: Background\")]\\n\\nThe *[Apology](/wiki/Apologetics \"Apologetics\")* was published in April 1642 as *An Apology against a Pamphlet Called a Modest Confutation of the Animadversions upon the Remonstrant against Smectymnvvs* and is [his final antiprelatical tract](/wiki/Milton%27s_antiprelatical_tracts \"Milton\\'s antiprelatical tracts\"). The tract was written as a response to a refutation by Bishop [Joseph Hall](/wiki/Joseph_Hall_(bishop) \"Joseph Hall (bishop)\").[[1]](#cite_note-1)\\n\\nTract\\n-----\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=2 \"Edit section: Tract\")]\\n\\nMilton argues that the defense of truth makes one vulnerable to personal attacks and emphasizes that role of personal integrity, especially his own:[[2]](#cite_note-2) \"as a member incorporate into that truth whereof I was perswaded\".[[3]](#cite_note-3) Milton defends his own integrity when he later writes:[[4]](#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) \"that indeed according to art is most eloquent, which returns and approaches neerest to nature from whence it came; and they expresse nature best, who in their lives least wander from her safe leading, which may be call\\'d regenerate reason\".[[5]](#cite_note-5) This idea is expanded further when he says:\\n\\n> he who would not be frustrated of his hope to write well hereafter in laudable things, ought him selfe to bee a true Poem, that is, a composition, and patterne of the best and honourable things; not presuming to sing high praises of heroick men, or famous Cities, unlesse he have in himselfe the experience and the practice of all that which is praise-worthy.[[6]](#cite_note-6)\\n\\nThemes\\n------\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=3 \"Edit section: Themes\")]\\n\\nThe *Apology*, like many of Milton\\'s other tracts, praises Parliament and emphasizes that they are reformers and the basis of the country.[[7]](#cite_note-7) The tract also connects truth of words with the individual\\'s character.[[4]](#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) Paul Stevens emphasizes that the tract reflects how \"Milton\\'s self is produced in the process of writing\" and that his self is put through \"a series of culturally approved *laterall* transformations\".[[8]](#cite_note-8) In particular, Elizabeth Wheeler points out that the tract contains \"Milton\\'s understanding of [Aristotle](/wiki/Aristotle \"Aristotle\")\\'s definition of man as a political animal. Heroism lies in the risk of changing and being changed in verbal exchange.\"[[9]](#cite_note-9)\\n\\nSee also\\n--------\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=4 \"Edit section: See also\")]\\n\\n* [Smectymnuus](/wiki/Smectymnuus \"Smectymnuus\")\\n\\nNotes\\n-----\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=5 \"Edit section: Notes\")]\\n\\n1. **[^](#cite_ref-1)** Wheeler 2003 p. 273\\n2. **[^](#cite_ref-2)** Wheeler 2003 pp. 273–274\\n3. **[^](#cite_ref-3)** Milton 1953 p. 871\\n4. ^ [***a***](#cite_ref-Wheeler_p._275_4-0) [***b***](#cite_ref-Wheeler_p._275_4-1) Wheeler 2003 p. 274\\n5. **[^](#cite_ref-5)** Milton 1953 p. 874\\n6. **[^](#cite_ref-6)** Milton 1953 p. 890\\n7. **[^](#cite_ref-7)** Keeble 2003 p. 132\\n8. **[^](#cite_ref-8)** Stevens 1988 p. 268\\n9. **[^](#cite_ref-9)** Wheeler 2003 p. 275\\n\\nReferences\\n----------\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=6 \"Edit section: References\")]\\n\\n* Keeble, N. From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

English Presbyterian leader (1600–1666)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/df/Edmund_Calamy_I.jpg/250px-Edmund_Calamy_I.jpg)](/wiki/File:Edmund_Calamy_I.jpg)

Edmund Calamy

**Edmund Calamy** (February 1600 – 29 October 1666) was an English [Presbyterian](/wiki/Presbyterian "Presbyterian") church leader and [divine](/wiki/Anglicanism#Anglican_divines "Anglicanism"). Known as **"the elder"**, he was the first of four generations of nonconformist ministers bearing the same name.

Early life
----------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Edmund_Calamy_the_Elder&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

The Calamy family claimed to be of [Huguenot](/wiki/Huguenot "Huguenot") descent. Edmund Calamy was born in the parish of [St Thomas the Apostle, London](/wiki/St_Thomas_the_Apostle,_London "St Thomas the Apostle, London"), and educated at [Merchant Taylors' School](/wiki/Merchant_Taylors%27_School,_Northwood "Merchant Taylors' School, Northwood") and then [Pembroke College, Cambridge](/wiki/Pembroke_College,_Cambridge "Pembroke College, Cambridge"),[[1]](#cite_note-1) where his opposition to [Arminianism](/wiki/Arminianism "Arminianism") excluded him from a fellowship. [Nicholas Felton](/wiki/Nicholas_Felton_(bishop) "Nicholas Felton (bishop)"), [Bishop of Ely](/wiki/Bishop_of_Ely "Bishop of Ely"), nevertheless made him his chaplain, and gave him the living of St Mary, [Swaffham Prior](/wiki/Swaffham_Prior "Swaffham Prior") in [East Cambridgeshire](/wiki/East_Cambridgeshire "East Cambridgeshire"), which he held till 1626.[[2]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911-2)

He then moved to [Bury St Edmunds](/wiki/Bury_St_Edmunds "Bury St Edmunds"), where he lectured for ten years; the later [Congregationalist](/wiki/Congregationalist_polity "Congregationalist polity") [Jeremiah Burroughs](/wiki/Jeremiah_Burroughs "Jeremiah Burroughs") was another preacher in the town.[[3]](#cite_note-3) He retired when his bishop [Matthew Wren](/wiki/Matthew_Wren "Matthew Wren") insisted on the observance of certain ceremonial articles: Calamy refused to read out the *[Book of Sports](/wiki/Book_of_Sports "Book of Sports")* in his church.[[4]](#cite_note-4) In 1636 he was appointed rector (or perhaps only lecturer) of [Rochford](/wiki/Rochford "Rochford") in [Essex](/wiki/Essex,_England "Essex, England"), but had to leave for the sake of his health. In 1639 he was elected to the perpetual curacy of [St Mary Aldermanbury](/wiki/St_Mary_Aldermanbury "St Mary Aldermanbury") in London, where he had a large following.[[2]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911-2)

Presbyterian activist
---------------------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Edmund_Calamy_the_Elder&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Presbyterian activist")]

At the opening of the [Long Parliament](/wiki/Long_Parliament "Long Parliament") he distinguished himself in defence of the [Presbyterian polity](/wiki/Presbyterian_polity "Presbyterian polity"), in contributing to the joint conciliatory work known as *[Smectymnuus](/wiki/Smectymnuus "Smectymnuus")*. It argued against Bishop [Joseph Hall](/wiki/Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)")'s presentation of [episcopacy](/wiki/Episcopacy "Episcopacy"), while articulating the Presbyterian positions. The initials of the names of the contributors formed the name under which it was published, viz., [Stephen Marshall](/wiki/Stephen_Marshall_(English_clergyman) "Stephen Marshall (English clergyman)") (SM), Edmund Calamy (EC), [Thomas Young](/wiki/Thomas_Young_(1587-1655) "Thomas Young (1587-1655)") (TY), [Matthew Newcomen](/wiki/Matthew_Newcomen "Matthew Newcomen") (MN), and [William Spurstow](/wiki/William_Spurstow "William Spurstow") (WS, then often written VVS equivalent to UUS).[[2]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911-2) These were clerical leaders of the Presbyterian movement within the [Church of England](/wiki/Church_of_England "Church of England"). At the same period Calamy was an influential evangelical preacher, calling in December 1641 for a preaching ministry throughout England.[[5]](#cite_note-5)

Calamy was an active member in the [Westminster Assembly](/wiki/Westminster_Assembly "Westminster Assembly") of divines, set up in 1643.[[2]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911-2) In that year he edited the *[Souldier's Pocket Bible](/wiki/Souldier%27s_Pocket_Bible "Souldier's Pocket Bible")*, a popular Biblical anthology designed for the Parliamentarian military forces.[[6]](#cite_note-SH-6)

The Smectymnuans were against [religious tolerance](/wiki/Religious_tolerance "Religious tolerance") and Calamy strongly advocated checking independent religious thinkers in 1644, attracting allies such as [Lazarus Seaman](/wiki/Lazarus_Seaman "Lazarus Seaman").[[7]](#cite_note-7) Refusing to advance to [Congregationalism](/wiki/Congregationalist_polity "Congregationalist polity"), he found within Presbyterianism a middle course which best suited his views of theology and church government.[[2]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911-2) Calamy belonged to the hypothetical universalist group in the Assembly, those influenced by [John Davenant](/wiki/John_Davenant "John Davenant") or his reading of the [Synod of Dort](/wiki/Synod_of_Dort "Synod of Dort"). [Richard Baxter](/wiki/Richard_Baxter "Richard Baxter") reported that Calamy, Lazarus, [Richard Vines](/wiki/Richard_Vines_(priest) "Richard Vines (priest)") and [John Arrowsmith](/wiki/John_Arrowsmith_(scholar) "John Arrowsmith (scholar)") were not hostile to [universal redemption](/wiki/Universal_redemption "Universal redemption").[[8]](#cite_note-8)

In 1647 he worked on the Assembly's Catechism.[[9]](#cite_note-9) In 1648 he was preaching at [St Benet Fink](/wiki/St_Benet_Fink "St Benet Fink"), to find an adversarial atmosphere in which the Baptist [Edward Barber](/wiki/Edward_Barber_(minister) "Edward Barber (minister)") had been invited to contradict him.[[10]](#cite_note-10)

He opposed the execution of King [Charles I](/wiki/Charles_I_of_England "Charles I of England"), and lived quietly under the Commonwealth.[[2]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911-2) Asked for advice by [Oliver Cromwell](/wiki/Oliver_Cromwell "Oliver Cromwell") on the dissolution of the [Rump Parliament](/wiki/Rump_Parliament "Rump Parliament") and the establishment of a Protectorate, he replied that nine out of ten would oppose it.[[11]](#cite_note-11)

After the Restoration
---------------------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Edmund_Calamy_the_Elder&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: After the Restoration")]

He was assiduous in promoting the return of [Charles II of England](/wiki/Charles_II_of_England "Charles II of England"), travelling to the Netherlands as one of the negotiators.[[6]](#cite_note-SH-6) After the [Restoration](/wiki/English_Restoration "English Restoration") in 1660 he was offered the [bishopric of Coventry and Lichfield](/wiki/Bishopric_of_Coventry_and_Lichfield "Bishopric of Coventry and Lichfield"), but declined it.[[2]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911-2) Presbyterians had warned him that his reputation and honour would suffer if he accepted, and he tried to co-ordinate a refusal with Richard Baxter, in the same position.[[12]](#cite_note-12)

He was made one of Charles's chaplains, and vainly tried to secure the legal ratification of Charles's declaration of 25 October 1660. He was ejected for [Nonconformity](/wiki/Nonconformist_(Protestantism) "Nonconformist (Protestantism)") in the [Great Ejection](/wiki/Great_Ejection "Great Ejection") of 1662, and was so affected by the sight of the devastation caused by the [Great Fire of London](/wiki/Great_Fire_of_London "Great Fire of London") that he died shortly afterwards. He was buried in the ruins of his church, near the place where the pulpit had stood.[[2]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911-2)

Calamy the Younger
------------------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Edmund_Calamy_the_Elder&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Calamy the Younger")]

Main article: [Edmund Calamy the Younger](/wiki/Edmund_Calamy_the_Younger "Edmund Calamy the Younger")

His eldest son was also called [Edmund Calamy](/wiki/Edmund_Calamy_the_Younger "Edmund Calamy the Younger"), known as "the Younger". Calamy the Younger followed a religious path similar to his father's, and lost the rectory of [Moreton, Essex](/wiki/Moreton,_Essex "Moreton, Essex") in the [Great Ejection](/wiki/Great_Ejection "Great Ejection") of 1662. He was of a retiring disposition and moderate views, and died in 1685. He was the father of the historian [Edmund Calamy](/wiki/Edmund_Calamy_(historian) "Edmund Calamy (historian)").[[14]](#cite_note-14)

**Stephen Marshall** (c. 1594 – 1655) was an [English](/wiki/England "England") [Nonconformist](/wiki/Nonconformist_(Protestantism) "Nonconformist (Protestantism)") churchman. His sermons, especially that on the death of [John Pym](/wiki/John_Pym "John Pym") in 1643, reveal eloquence and fervour. The only "systematic" work he published was *A Defence of [Infant Baptism](/wiki/Infant_Baptism "Infant Baptism")*, against [John Tombes](/wiki/John_Tombes "John Tombes") (1646).

Early life
----------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Stephen_Marshall_(minister)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

He was born at [Godmanchester](/wiki/Godmanchester "Godmanchester") in [Huntingdonshire](/wiki/Huntingdonshire "Huntingdonshire"), and was educated at [Emmanuel College, Cambridge](/wiki/Emmanuel_College,_Cambridge "Emmanuel College, Cambridge") (M.A. 1622, B.D. 1629). After holding the living of [Wethersfield](/wiki/Wethersfield,_Essex "Wethersfield, Essex") in [Essex](/wiki/Essex,_England "Essex, England"), he became vicar of [Finchingfield](/wiki/Finchingfield "Finchingfield"). In 1636 he was reported for "want of conformity."

Civil War years
---------------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Stephen_Marshall_(minister)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Civil War years")]

Marshall was a powerful preacher: [Robert Baillie](/wiki/Robert_Baillie "Robert Baillie") noted that he was reckoned the best in England.[[1]](#cite_note-1) He also influenced the elections for the [Short Parliament](/wiki/Short_Parliament "Short Parliament") of 1640: [Edward Hyde, 1st Earl of Clarendon](/wiki/Edward_Hyde,_1st_Earl_of_Clarendon "Edward Hyde, 1st Earl of Clarendon") considered his influence on the parliamentary side to be greater than that of [William Laud](/wiki/William_Laud "William Laud") on the royalist. In 1642 Marshall was appointed lecturer at [St Margaret's, Westminster](/wiki/St._Margaret%27s,_Westminster "St. Margaret's, Westminster"), and delivered a series of addresses to the Commons in which he advocated episcopal and liturgical reform.

He had a share in writing *[Smectymnuus](/wiki/Smectymnuus "Smectymnuus")*, was appointed chaplain to the [Earl of Essex's regiment](/wiki/Earl_of_Essex%27s_regiment "Earl of Essex's regiment") in 1642, and a member of the [Westminster Assembly](/wiki/Westminster_Assembly "Westminster Assembly") in 1643. He represented the English Parliament in [Scotland](/wiki/Scotland "Scotland") in 1643, and attended the parliamentary commissions at the [Uxbridge Conference](/wiki/Uxbridge_Conference "Uxbridge Conference") in 1645. He was with Archbishop Laud before the latter's execution, and was chaplain to King [Charles I](/wiki/Charles_I_of_England "Charles I of England") at [Holmby House](/wiki/Holmby_House "Holmby House") and at [Carisbrooke Castle](/wiki/Carisbrooke_Castle "Carisbrooke Castle").

Later life
----------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Stephen_Marshall_(minister)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Later life")]

A moderate [Presbyterian](/wiki/Presbyterian "Presbyterian"), he contributed to the [Westminster Shorter Catechism](/wiki/Westminster_Shorter_Catechism "Westminster Shorter Catechism") in 1647, and was one of the "Triers" in 1654. He died in November 1655 and was buried in [Westminster Abbey](/wiki/Westminster_Abbey "Westminster Abbey"), but his body was exhumed and maltreated at the [Restoration](/wiki/English_Restoration "English Restoration").

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

English minister (d. 1669)

**Matthew Newcomen** (c. 1610 – 1 September 1669) was an [English](/wiki/England "England") [nonconformist](/wiki/Nonconformist_(Protestantism) "Nonconformist (Protestantism)") churchman.[[1]](#cite_note-1)

His exact date of birth is unknown. He was educated at [St John's College, Cambridge](/wiki/St_John%27s_College,_Cambridge "St John's College, Cambridge") (M.A. 1633).[[2]](#cite_note-2) In 1636 he became lecturer at [Dedham](/wiki/Dedham,_Essex "Dedham, Essex") in [Essex](/wiki/Essex,_England "Essex, England"), and led the church reform party in that county. He assisted [Edmund Calamy the Elder](/wiki/Edmund_Calamy_the_Elder "Edmund Calamy the Elder") in writing *[Smectymnuus](/wiki/Smectymnuus "Smectymnuus")* (1641), and preached before parliament in 1643. He was multi-talented, excelling in preaching and debate, and was offered several lucrative positions.

He protested against the extreme democratic proposals called *[The Agreement of the People](/wiki/The_Agreement_of_the_People "The Agreement of the People")* (1647), and was one of the commissioners at the [Savoy Synod](/wiki/Savoy_Synod "Savoy Synod") of 1658. When the [Act of Uniformity](/wiki/Act_of_Uniformity_1662 "Act of Uniformity 1662") was passed in 1662, Newcomen lost his living, but was soon invited to the pastorate at [Leiden](/wiki/Leiden "Leiden"), where he was held in high esteem not only by his own people but by the university professors. He died of [plague](/wiki/Bubonic_plague "Bubonic plague") in 1669.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

(Redirected from [William Spurstow](/w/index.php?title=William_Spurstow&redirect=no "William Spurstow"))

English clergyman and theologian (d. 1666)

For the MP in the Long Parliament died 1644, see [William Spurstow (merchant)](/wiki/William_Spurstow_(merchant) "William Spurstow (merchant)").

**William Spurstowe** (Spurstow) (c. 1605–1666) was an English clergyman, theologian, and member of the [Westminster Assembly](/wiki/Westminster_Assembly "Westminster Assembly"). He was one of the [Smectymnuus](/wiki/Smectymnuus "Smectymnuus") group of Presbyterian clergy, supplying the final WS (read as UUS) of the acronym.

Life
----

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=William_Spurstowe&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Life")]

His father [William Spurstow](/wiki/William_Spurstow_(merchant) "William Spurstow (merchant)") was a mercer in London. The son studied at [Emmanuel College, Cambridge](/wiki/Emmanuel_College,_Cambridge "Emmanuel College, Cambridge").[[1]](#cite_note-1)[[2]](#cite_note-2)

He became a Fellow of [St. Katherine's Hall College, Cambridge](/wiki/St._Katherine%27s_Hall_College,_Cambridge "St. Katherine's Hall College, Cambridge") in 1638, during the Mastership of [Ralph Brownrigg](/wiki/Ralph_Brownrigg "Ralph Brownrigg"), and succeeded as [Master in 1645](/wiki/List_of_Masters_of_St_Catharine%27s_College,_Cambridge "List of Masters of St Catharine's College, Cambridge"). At the time it was strongly Puritan in tone, with [John Arrowsmith](/wiki/John_Arrowsmith_(scholar) "John Arrowsmith (scholar)"), [John Bond](/wiki/John_Bond_(Puritan) "John Bond (Puritan)"), [Thomas Goodwin](/wiki/Thomas_Goodwin "Thomas Goodwin"), [Andrew Perne](/wiki/Andrew_Perne_(c.1595%E2%80%931654) "Andrew Perne (c.1595–1654)") and [William Strong](/wiki/William_Strong_(d._1654) "William Strong (d. 1654)") as other Fellows.[[3]](#cite_note-3)[[4]](#cite_note-4)[[5]](#cite_note-5)

In the late 1630s he was an associate of [John Hampden](/wiki/John_Hampden "John Hampden"), and in 1638 he became vicar of [Great Hampden](/wiki/Great_Hampden "Great Hampden").[[6]](#cite_note-6)[[7]](#cite_note-7) Later he was chaplain to Hampden's troops.[[8]](#cite_note-8)

He became vicar of [Hackney](/wiki/Hackney_(parish) "Hackney (parish)") in 1643, and was made Master of his college. He was deprived of the mastership, in 1650.[[9]](#cite_note-9)

After the Restoration, he was consulted on the *[Declaration of Indulgence](/wiki/Declaration_of_Indulgence_(1672) "Declaration of Indulgence (1672)")*.[[10]](#cite_note-10) He was ejected from his parish of Hackney for nonconformity, in 1662. He remained in Hackney, welcomed [Richard Baxter](/wiki/Richard_Baxter "Richard Baxter"), employed [Ezekiel Hopkins](/wiki/Ezekiel_Hopkins "Ezekiel Hopkins"), and provided a focus for numerous other ejected ministers.[[11]](#cite_note-11) He built six [almshouses](/wiki/Almshouse "Almshouse") there, work starting shortly before his death.[[12]](#cite_note-12)

Works
-----

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=William_Spurstowe&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Works")]

* *Englands Patterne and Duty in Its Monthly Fasts* (1643)
* *Englands eminent judgments, caus'd by the abuse of Gods eminent mercies* (1644)
* *The Magistrate's Dignity and Duty* (1653)
* [*The Wels of Salvation Opened*](https://books.google.com/books?id=LQU8AQAAMAAJ). London: T.R. & E.M. 1655.
* *Death and the Grave No Bar to Believers Happinesse* (1656)
* *A Crown of Life, the Reward of Faithfulnesse* (1662)
* [*The Spiritual Chymist; Or, Six Decads of Divine Meditations on Several Subjects*](https://books.google.com/books?id=JMB8SwCrq8wC). 1666.
* [*The Wiles of Satan*](https://books.google.com/books?id=s81ir2z7Rr4C). 1666.
* [*Tract Entitled True and Faithful Relation of a Worthy Discourse: Between Colonel John Hampden and Colonel Oliver Cromwell*](https://archive.org/details/tractentitledtru00londrich). Chapman and Hall. 1847.

**Stephen Marshall** (c. 1594 – 1655) was an [English](/wiki/England "England") [Nonconformist](/wiki/Nonconformist_(Protestantism) "Nonconformist (Protestantism)") churchman. His sermons, especially that on the death of [John Pym](/wiki/John_Pym "John Pym") in 1643, reveal eloquence and fervour. The only "systematic" work he published was *A Defence of [Infant Baptism](/wiki/Infant_Baptism "Infant Baptism")*, against [John Tombes](/wiki/John_Tombes "John Tombes") (1646).

Early life
----------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Stephen_Marshall_(minister)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

He was born at [Godmanchester](/wiki/Godmanchester "Godmanchester") in [Huntingdonshire](/wiki/Huntingdonshire "Huntingdonshire"), and was educated at [Emmanuel College, Cambridge](/wiki/Emmanuel_College,_Cambridge "Emmanuel College, Cambridge") (M.A. 1622, B.D. 1629). After holding the living of [Wethersfield](/wiki/Wethersfield,_Essex "Wethersfield, Essex") in [Essex](/wiki/Essex,_England "Essex, England"), he became vicar of [Finchingfield](/wiki/Finchingfield "Finchingfield"). In 1636 he was reported for "want of conformity."

Civil War years
---------------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Stephen_Marshall_(minister)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Civil War years")]

Marshall was a powerful preacher: [Robert Baillie](/wiki/Robert_Baillie "Robert Baillie") noted that he was reckoned the best in England.[[1]](#cite_note-1) He also influenced the elections for the [Short Parliament](/wiki/Short_Parliament "Short Parliament") of 1640: [Edward Hyde, 1st Earl of Clarendon](/wiki/Edward_Hyde,_1st_Earl_of_Clarendon "Edward Hyde, 1st Earl of Clarendon") considered his influence on the parliamentary side to be greater than that of [William Laud](/wiki/William_Laud "William Laud") on the royalist. In 1642 Marshall was appointed lecturer at [St Margaret's, Westminster](/wiki/St._Margaret%27s,_Westminster "St. Margaret's, Westminster"), and delivered a series of addresses to the Commons in which he advocated episcopal and liturgical reform.

He had a share in writing *[Smectymnuus](/wiki/Smectymnuus "Smectymnuus")*, was appointed chaplain to the [Earl of Essex's regiment](/wiki/Earl_of_Essex%27s_regiment "Earl of Essex's regiment") in 1642, and a member of the [Westminster Assembly](/wiki/Westminster_Assembly "Westminster Assembly") in 1643. He represented the English Parliament in [Scotland](/wiki/Scotland "Scotland") in 1643, and attended the parliamentary commissions at the [Uxbridge Conference](/wiki/Uxbridge_Conference "Uxbridge Conference") in 1645. He was with Archbishop Laud before the latter's execution, and was chaplain to King [Charles I](/wiki/Charles_I_of_England "Charles I of England") at [Holmby House](/wiki/Holmby_House "Holmby House") and at [Carisbrooke Castle](/wiki/Carisbrooke_Castle "Carisbrooke Castle").

Later life
----------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Stephen_Marshall_(minister)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Later life")]

A moderate [Presbyterian](/wiki/Presbyterian "Presbyterian"), he contributed to the [Westminster Shorter Catechism](/wiki/Westminster_Shorter_Catechism "Westminster Shorter Catechism") in 1647, and was one of the "Triers" in 1654. He died in November 1655 and was buried in [Westminster Abbey](/wiki/Westminster_Abbey "Westminster Abbey"), but his body was exhumed and maltreated at the [Restoration](/wiki/English_Restoration "English Restoration").

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

English Presbyterian leader (1600–1666)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/df/Edmund_Calamy_I.jpg/250px-Edmund_Calamy_I.jpg)](/wiki/File:Edmund_Calamy_I.jpg)

Edmund Calamy

**Edmund Calamy** (February 1600 – 29 October 1666) was an English [Presbyterian](/wiki/Presbyterian "Presbyterian") church leader and [divine](/wiki/Anglicanism#Anglican_divines "Anglicanism"). Known as **"the elder"**, he was the first of four generations of nonconformist ministers bearing the same name.

Early life
----------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Edmund_Calamy_the_Elder&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

The Calamy family claimed to be of [Huguenot](/wiki/Huguenot "Huguenot") descent. Edmund Calamy was born in the parish of [St Thomas the Apostle, London](/wiki/St_Thomas_the_Apostle,_London "St Thomas the Apostle, London"), and educated at [Merchant Taylors' School](/wiki/Merchant_Taylors%27_School,_Northwood "Merchant Taylors' School, Northwood") and then [Pembroke College, Cambridge](/wiki/Pembroke_College,_Cambridge "Pembroke College, Cambridge"),[[1]](#cite_note-1) where his opposition to [Arminianism](/wiki/Arminianism "Arminianism") excluded him from a fellowship. [Nicholas Felton](/wiki/Nicholas_Felton_(bishop) "Nicholas Felton (bishop)"), [Bishop of Ely](/wiki/Bishop_of_Ely "Bishop of Ely"), nevertheless made him his chaplain, and gave him the living of St Mary, [Swaffham Prior](/wiki/Swaffham_Prior "Swaffham Prior") in [East Cambridgeshire](/wiki/East_Cambridgeshire "East Cambridgeshire"), which he held till 1626.[[2]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911-2)

He then moved to [Bury St Edmunds](/wiki/Bury_St_Edmunds "Bury St Edmunds"), where he lectured for ten years; the later [Congregationalist](/wiki/Congregationalist_polity "Congregationalist polity") [Jeremiah Burroughs](/wiki/Jeremiah_Burroughs "Jeremiah Burroughs") was another preacher in the town.[[3]](#cite_note-3) He retired when his bishop [Matthew Wren](/wiki/Matthew_Wren "Matthew Wren") insisted on the observance of certain ceremonial articles: Calamy refused to read out the *[Book of Sports](/wiki/Book_of_Sports "Book of Sports")* in his church.[[4]](#cite_note-4) In 1636 he was appointed rector (or perhaps only lecturer) of [Rochford](/wiki/Rochford "Rochford") in [Essex](/wiki/Essex,_England "Essex, England"), but had to leave for the sake of his health. In 1639 he was elected to the perpetual curacy of [St Mary Aldermanbury](/wiki/St_Mary_Aldermanbury "St Mary Aldermanbury") in London, where he had a large following.[[2]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911-2)

Presbyterian activist
---------------------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Edmund_Calamy_the_Elder&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Presbyterian activist")]

At the opening of the [Long Parliament](/wiki/Long_Parliament "Long Parliament") he distinguished himself in defence of the [Presbyterian polity](/wiki/Presbyterian_polity "Presbyterian polity"), in contributing to the joint conciliatory work known as *[Smectymnuus](/wiki/Smectymnuus "Smectymnuus")*. It argued against Bishop [Joseph Hall](/wiki/Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)")'s presentation of [episcopacy](/wiki/Episcopacy "Episcopacy"), while articulating the Presbyterian positions. The initials of the names of the contributors formed the name under which it was published, viz., [Stephen Marshall](/wiki/Stephen_Marshall_(English_clergyman) "Stephen Marshall (English clergyman)") (SM), Edmund Calamy (EC), [Thomas Young](/wiki/Thomas_Young_(1587-1655) "Thomas Young (1587-1655)") (TY), [Matthew Newcomen](/wiki/Matthew_Newcomen "Matthew Newcomen") (MN), and [William Spurstow](/wiki/William_Spurstow "William Spurstow") (WS, then often written VVS equivalent to UUS).[[2]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911-2) These were clerical leaders of the Presbyterian movement within the [Church of England](/wiki/Church_of_England "Church of England"). At the same period Calamy was an influential evangelical preacher, calling in December 1641 for a preaching ministry throughout England.[[5]](#cite_note-5)

Calamy was an active member in the [Westminster Assembly](/wiki/Westminster_Assembly "Westminster Assembly") of divines, set up in 1643.[[2]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911-2) In that year he edited the *[Souldier's Pocket Bible](/wiki/Souldier%27s_Pocket_Bible "Souldier's Pocket Bible")*, a popular Biblical anthology designed for the Parliamentarian military forces.[[6]](#cite_note-SH-6)

The Smectymnuans were against [religious tolerance](/wiki/Religious_tolerance "Religious tolerance") and Calamy strongly advocated checking independent religious thinkers in 1644, attracting allies such as [Lazarus Seaman](/wiki/Lazarus_Seaman "Lazarus Seaman").[[7]](#cite_note-7) Refusing to advance to [Congregationalism](/wiki/Congregationalist_polity "Congregationalist polity"), he found within Presbyterianism a middle course which best suited his views of theology and church government.[[2]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911-2) Calamy belonged to the hypothetical universalist group in the Assembly, those influenced by [John Davenant](/wiki/John_Davenant "John Davenant") or his reading of the [Synod of Dort](/wiki/Synod_of_Dort "Synod of Dort"). [Richard Baxter](/wiki/Richard_Baxter "Richard Baxter") reported that Calamy, Lazarus, [Richard Vines](/wiki/Richard_Vines_(priest) "Richard Vines (priest)") and [John Arrowsmith](/wiki/John_Arrowsmith_(scholar) "John Arrowsmith (scholar)") were not hostile to [universal redemption](/wiki/Universal_redemption "Universal redemption").[[8]](#cite_note-8)

In 1647 he worked on the Assembly's Catechism.[[9]](#cite_note-9) In 1648 he was preaching at [St Benet Fink](/wiki/St_Benet_Fink "St Benet Fink"), to find an adversarial atmosphere in which the Baptist [Edward Barber](/wiki/Edward_Barber_(minister) "Edward Barber (minister)") had been invited to contradict him.[[10]](#cite_note-10)

He opposed the execution of King [Charles I](/wiki/Charles_I_of_England "Charles I of England"), and lived quietly under the Commonwealth.[[2]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911-2) Asked for advice by [Oliver Cromwell](/wiki/Oliver_Cromwell "Oliver Cromwell") on the dissolution of the [Rump Parliament](/wiki/Rump_Parliament "Rump Parliament") and the establishment of a Protectorate, he replied that nine out of ten would oppose it.[[11]](#cite_note-11)

After the Restoration
---------------------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Edmund_Calamy_the_Elder&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: After the Restoration")]

He was assiduous in promoting the return of [Charles II of England](/wiki/Charles_II_of_England "Charles II of England"), travelling to the Netherlands as one of the negotiators.[[6]](#cite_note-SH-6) After the [Restoration](/wiki/English_Restoration "English Restoration") in 1660 he was offered the [bishopric of Coventry and Lichfield](/wiki/Bishopric_of_Coventry_and_Lichfield "Bishopric of Coventry and Lichfield"), but declined it.[[2]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911-2) Presbyterians had warned him that his reputation and honour would suffer if he accepted, and he tried to co-ordinate a refusal with Richard Baxter, in the same position.[[12]](#cite_note-12)

He was made one of Charles's chaplains, and vainly tried to secure the legal ratification of Charles's declaration of 25 October 1660. He was ejected for [Nonconformity](/wiki/Nonconformist_(Protestantism) "Nonconformist (Protestantism)") in the [Great Ejection](/wiki/Great_Ejection "Great Ejection") of 1662, and was so affected by the sight of the devastation caused by the [Great Fire of London](/wiki/Great_Fire_of_London "Great Fire of London") that he died shortly afterwards. He was buried in the ruins of his church, near the place where the pulpit had stood.[[2]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911-2)

Works
-----

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Edmund_Calamy_the_Elder&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Works")]

His publications are almost entirely sermons.[[13]](#cite_note-13)

* [*The Art of Divine Meditation*](https://quod.lib.umich.edu/e/eebo/A31893.0001.001?view=toc) (London: for Tho. Parkhurst, 1634) – not sermons.
* [*An Answer to a Book entitled, An Humble Remonstrance*](https://quod.lib.umich.edu/e/eebo/A52055.0001.001?view=toc) (1641) as a member of *[Smectymnuus](/wiki/Smectymnuus "Smectymnuus")*
* [*Gods Free Mercy to England*](https://quod.lib.umich.edu/e/eebo/A32016.0001.001?view=toc) (1642)
* [*Englands Looking-glasse*](https://quod.lib.umich.edu/e/eebo/A31933.0001.001?view=toc) (1642)
* *Souldier's Pocket Bible* (1643), editor ([1895 reprint](https://catalog.hathitrust.org/Record/001409086))
* [*Jus Divinum Ministerii Evangelici*](https://quod.lib.umich.edu/cgi/t/text/text-idx?c=eebo;idno=A46373.0001.001) (1654)
* [*The Godly Man's Ark*](https://quod.lib.umich.edu/e/eebo/A31997.0001.001?view=toc) (1658)

Calamy the Younger
------------------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Edmund_Calamy_the_Elder&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Calamy the Younger")]

Main article: [Edmund Calamy the Younger](/wiki/Edmund_Calamy_the_Younger "Edmund Calamy the Younger")

His eldest son was also called [Edmund Calamy](/wiki/Edmund_Calamy_the_Younger "Edmund Calamy the Younger"), known as "the Younger". Calamy the Younger followed a religious path similar to his father's, and lost the rectory of [Moreton, Essex](/wiki/Moreton,_Essex "Moreton, Essex") in the [Great Ejection](/wiki/Great_Ejection "Great Ejection") of 1662. He was of a retiring disposition and moderate views, and died in 1685. He was the father of the historian [Edmund Calamy](/wiki/Edmund_Calamy_(historian) "Edmund Calamy (historian)").[[14]](#cite_note-14)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

English minister (d. 1669)

**Matthew Newcomen** (c. 1610 – 1 September 1669) was an [English](/wiki/England "England") [nonconformist](/wiki/Nonconformist_(Protestantism) "Nonconformist (Protestantism)") churchman.[[1]](#cite_note-1)

His exact date of birth is unknown. He was educated at [St John's College, Cambridge](/wiki/St_John%27s_College,_Cambridge "St John's College, Cambridge") (M.A. 1633).[[2]](#cite_note-2) In 1636 he became lecturer at [Dedham](/wiki/Dedham,_Essex "Dedham, Essex") in [Essex](/wiki/Essex,_England "Essex, England"), and led the church reform party in that county. He assisted [Edmund Calamy the Elder](/wiki/Edmund_Calamy_the_Elder "Edmund Calamy the Elder") in writing *[Smectymnuus](/wiki/Smectymnuus "Smectymnuus")* (1641), and preached before parliament in 1643. He was multi-talented, excelling in preaching and debate, and was offered several lucrative positions.

He protested against the extreme democratic proposals called *[The Agreement of the People](/wiki/The_Agreement_of_the_People "The Agreement of the People")* (1647), and was one of the commissioners at the [Savoy Synod](/wiki/Savoy_Synod "Savoy Synod") of 1658. When the [Act of Uniformity](/wiki/Act_of_Uniformity_1662 "Act of Uniformity 1662") was passed in 1662, Newcomen lost his living, but was soon invited to the pastorate at [Leiden](/wiki/Leiden "Leiden"), where he was held in high esteem not only by his own people but by the university professors. He died of [plague](/wiki/Bubonic_plague "Bubonic plague") in 1669.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

(Redirected from [William Spurstow](/w/index.php?title=William_Spurstow&redirect=no "William Spurstow"))

English clergyman and theologian (d. 1666)

For the MP in the Long Parliament died 1644, see [William Spurstow (merchant)](/wiki/William_Spurstow_(merchant) "William Spurstow (merchant)").

**William Spurstowe** (Spurstow) (c. 1605–1666) was an English clergyman, theologian, and member of the [Westminster Assembly](/wiki/Westminster_Assembly "Westminster Assembly"). He was one of the [Smectymnuus](/wiki/Smectymnuus "Smectymnuus") group of Presbyterian clergy, supplying the final WS (read as UUS) of the acronym.

Life
----

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=William_Spurstowe&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Life")]

His father [William Spurstow](/wiki/William_Spurstow_(merchant) "William Spurstow (merchant)") was a mercer in London. The son studied at [Emmanuel College, Cambridge](/wiki/Emmanuel_College,_Cambridge "Emmanuel College, Cambridge").[[1]](#cite_note-1)[[2]](#cite_note-2)

He became a Fellow of [St. Katherine's Hall College, Cambridge](/wiki/St._Katherine%27s_Hall_College,_Cambridge "St. Katherine's Hall College, Cambridge") in 1638, during the Mastership of [Ralph Brownrigg](/wiki/Ralph_Brownrigg "Ralph Brownrigg"), and succeeded as [Master in 1645](/wiki/List_of_Masters_of_St_Catharine%27s_College,_Cambridge "List of Masters of St Catharine's College, Cambridge"). At the time it was strongly Puritan in tone, with [John Arrowsmith](/wiki/John_Arrowsmith_(scholar) "John Arrowsmith (scholar)"), [John Bond](/wiki/John_Bond_(Puritan) "John Bond (Puritan)"), [Thomas Goodwin](/wiki/Thomas_Goodwin "Thomas Goodwin"), [Andrew Perne](/wiki/Andrew_Perne_(c.1595%E2%80%931654) "Andrew Perne (c.1595–1654)") and [William Strong](/wiki/William_Strong_(d._1654) "William Strong (d. 1654)") as other Fellows.[[3]](#cite_note-3)[[4]](#cite_note-4)[[5]](#cite_note-5)

In the late 1630s he was an associate of [John Hampden](/wiki/John_Hampden "John Hampden"), and in 1638 he became vicar of [Great Hampden](/wiki/Great_Hampden "Great Hampden").[[6]](#cite_note-6)[[7]](#cite_note-7) Later he was chaplain to Hampden's troops.[[8]](#cite_note-8)

He became vicar of [Hackney](/wiki/Hackney_(parish) "Hackney (parish)") in 1643, and was made Master of his college. He was deprived of the mastership, in 1650.[[9]](#cite_note-9)

After the Restoration, he was consulted on the *[Declaration of Indulgence](/wiki/Declaration_of_Indulgence_(1672) "Declaration of Indulgence (1672)")*.[[10]](#cite_note-10) He was ejected from his parish of Hackney for nonconformity, in 1662. He remained in Hackney, welcomed [Richard Baxter](/wiki/Richard_Baxter "Richard Baxter"), employed [Ezekiel Hopkins](/wiki/Ezekiel_Hopkins "Ezekiel Hopkins"), and provided a focus for numerous other ejected ministers.[[11]](#cite_note-11) He built six [almshouses](/wiki/Almshouse "Almshouse") there, work starting shortly before his death.[[12]](#cite_note-12)

Works
-----

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=William_Spurstowe&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Works")]

* *Englands Patterne and Duty in Its Monthly Fasts* (1643)
* *Englands eminent judgments, caus'd by the abuse of Gods eminent mercies* (1644)
* *The Magistrate's Dignity and Duty* (1653)
* [*The Wels of Salvation Opened*](https://books.google.com/books?id=LQU8AQAAMAAJ). London: T.R. & E.M. 1655.
* *Death and the Grave No Bar to Believers Happinesse* (1656)
* *A Crown of Life, the Reward of Faithfulnesse* (1662)
* [*The Spiritual Chymist; Or, Six Decads of Divine Meditations on Several Subjects*](https://books.google.com/books?id=JMB8SwCrq8wC). 1666.
* [*The Wiles of Satan*](https://books.google.com/books?id=s81ir2z7Rr4C). 1666.
* [*Tract Entitled True and Faithful Relation of a Worthy Discourse: Between Colonel John Hampden and Colonel Oliver Cromwell*](https://archive.org/details/tractentitledtru00londrich). Chapman and Hall. 1847.

***Apology for Smectymnuus***, or *An Apology for a Pamphlet*, was published by [John Milton](/wiki/John_Milton "John Milton") in April 1642. It was the final of his [antiprelatical tracts](/wiki/Milton%27s_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts") which criticize the structure of the [Church of England](/wiki/Church_of_England "Church of England").

Background
----------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background")]

The *[Apology](/wiki/Apologetics "Apologetics")* was published in April 1642 as *An Apology against a Pamphlet Called a Modest Confutation of the Animadversions upon the Remonstrant against Smectymnvvs* and is [his final antiprelatical tract](/wiki/Milton%27s_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts"). The tract was written as a response to a refutation by Bishop [Joseph Hall](/wiki/Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)").[[1]](#cite_note-1)

Tract
-----

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Tract")]

Milton argues that the defense of truth makes one vulnerable to personal attacks and emphasizes that role of personal integrity, especially his own:[[2]](#cite_note-2) "as a member incorporate into that truth whereof I was perswaded".[[3]](#cite_note-3) Milton defends his own integrity when he later writes:[[4]](#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) "that indeed according to art is most eloquent, which returns and approaches neerest to nature from whence it came; and they expresse nature best, who in their lives least wander from her safe leading, which may be call'd regenerate reason".[[5]](#cite_note-5) This idea is expanded further when he says:

> he who would not be frustrated of his hope to write well hereafter in laudable things, ought him selfe to bee a true Poem, that is, a composition, and patterne of the best and honourable things; not presuming to sing high praises of heroick men, or famous Cities, unlesse he have in himselfe the experience and the practice of all that which is praise-worthy.[[6]](#cite_note-6)

Themes
------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Themes")]

The *Apology*, like many of Milton's other tracts, praises Parliament and emphasizes that they are reformers and the basis of the country.[[7]](#cite_note-7) The tract also connects truth of words with the individual's character.[[4]](#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) Paul Stevens emphasizes that the tract reflects how "Milton's self is produced in the process of writing" and that his self is put through "a series of culturally approved *laterall* transformations".[[8]](#cite_note-8) In particular, Elizabeth Wheeler points out that the tract contains "Milton's understanding of [Aristotle](/wiki/Aristotle "Aristotle")'s definition of man as a political animal. Heroism lies in the risk of changing and being changed in verbal exchange."[[9]](#cite_note-9)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Group of clergy active in 1641 England

**Smectymnuus** was the *[nom de plume](/wiki/Pen_name "Pen name")* of a group of [Puritan](/wiki/Puritan "Puritan") clergymen active in [England](/wiki/England "England") in 1641 during the reign of [Charles I](/wiki/Charles_I_of_England,_Scotland,_and_Ireland "Charles I of England, Scotland, and Ireland"). It comprised four leading English churchmen, and one Scottish minister ([Thomas Young](/wiki/Thomas_Young_(1587-1655) "Thomas Young (1587-1655)")). They went on to provide leadership for the anti-episcopal forces in the [Church of England](/wiki/Church_of_England "Church of England"), continuing into the [Westminster Assembly](/wiki/Westminster_Assembly "Westminster Assembly"), where they also opposed the Independent movement.

The name is an acronym derived from the initials of the five authors: [Stephen Marshall](/wiki/Stephen_Marshall_(English_clergyman) "Stephen Marshall (English clergyman)"), [Edmund Calamy](/wiki/Edmund_Calamy_the_Elder "Edmund Calamy the Elder"), Thomas Young, [Matthew Newcomen](/wiki/Matthew_Newcomen "Matthew Newcomen"), and [William Spurstow](/wiki/William_Spurstow "William Spurstow"). Their first pamphlet, *An Answer to a booke entituled, An Humble Remonstrance. In Which, the Original of Liturgy and Episcopacy is discussed*, appeared in March 1641. The pamphlet was written in response to [Joseph Hall's](/wiki/Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)") *An Humble Remonstrance to the High Court of Parliament*. It is thought that [John Milton](/wiki/John_Milton "John Milton") wrote the postscript for Smectymnuus's reply.[[1]](#cite_note-1)

This response provoked Hall to write another reply: *A Defence of the Humble Remonstrance, against the Frivolous and false Expectations of Smectymnuus*. Smectymnuus answered Hall again with their *A Vindication of the Answer to the Humble Remonstrance, from the Unjust Imputations of Frivolousnesse and Falsehood*.

Milton also published two tracts defending the Smectymnuus group from Hall: *[Animadversions upon The Remonstrants Defence Against Smectymnvvs](/wiki/Animadversions "Animadversions")* (1641) and *[Apology for Smectymnuus](/wiki/Apology_for_Smectymnuus "Apology for Smectymnuus")* (1642).[[2]](#cite_note-2) Thomas Young was a former tutor and close friend to Milton.[[3]](#cite_note-3)

**Stephen Marshall** (c. 1594 – 1655) was an [English](/wiki/England "England") [Nonconformist](/wiki/Nonconformist_(Protestantism) "Nonconformist (Protestantism)") churchman. His sermons, especially that on the death of [John Pym](/wiki/John_Pym "John Pym") in 1643, reveal eloquence and fervour. The only "systematic" work he published was *A Defence of [Infant Baptism](/wiki/Infant_Baptism "Infant Baptism")*, against [John Tombes](/wiki/John_Tombes "John Tombes") (1646).

Early life
----------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Stephen_Marshall_(minister)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

He was born at [Godmanchester](/wiki/Godmanchester "Godmanchester") in [Huntingdonshire](/wiki/Huntingdonshire "Huntingdonshire"), and was educated at [Emmanuel College, Cambridge](/wiki/Emmanuel_College,_Cambridge "Emmanuel College, Cambridge") (M.A. 1622, B.D. 1629). After holding the living of [Wethersfield](/wiki/Wethersfield,_Essex "Wethersfield, Essex") in [Essex](/wiki/Essex,_England "Essex, England"), he became vicar of [Finchingfield](/wiki/Finchingfield "Finchingfield"). In 1636 he was reported for "want of conformity."

Civil War years
---------------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Stephen_Marshall_(minister)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Civil War years")]

Marshall was a powerful preacher: [Robert Baillie](/wiki/Robert_Baillie "Robert Baillie") noted that he was reckoned the best in England.[[1]](#cite_note-1) He also influenced the elections for the [Short Parliament](/wiki/Short_Parliament "Short Parliament") of 1640: [Edward Hyde, 1st Earl of Clarendon](/wiki/Edward_Hyde,_1st_Earl_of_Clarendon "Edward Hyde, 1st Earl of Clarendon") considered his influence on the parliamentary side to be greater than that of [William Laud](/wiki/William_Laud "William Laud") on the royalist. In 1642 Marshall was appointed lecturer at [St Margaret's, Westminster](/wiki/St._Margaret%27s,_Westminster "St. Margaret's, Westminster"), and delivered a series of addresses to the Commons in which he advocated episcopal and liturgical reform.

He had a share in writing *[Smectymnuus](/wiki/Smectymnuus "Smectymnuus")*, was appointed chaplain to the [Earl of Essex's regiment](/wiki/Earl_of_Essex%27s_regiment "Earl of Essex's regiment") in 1642, and a member of the [Westminster Assembly](/wiki/Westminster_Assembly "Westminster Assembly") in 1643. He represented the English Parliament in [Scotland](/wiki/Scotland "Scotland") in 1643, and attended the parliamentary commissions at the [Uxbridge Conference](/wiki/Uxbridge_Conference "Uxbridge Conference") in 1645. He was with Archbishop Laud before the latter's execution, and was chaplain to King [Charles I](/wiki/Charles_I_of_England "Charles I of England") at [Holmby House](/wiki/Holmby_House "Holmby House") and at [Carisbrooke Castle](/wiki/Carisbrooke_Castle "Carisbrooke Castle").

Later life
----------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Stephen_Marshall_(minister)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Later life")]

A moderate [Presbyterian](/wiki/Presbyterian "Presbyterian"), he contributed to the [Westminster Shorter Catechism](/wiki/Westminster_Shorter_Catechism "Westminster Shorter Catechism") in 1647, and was one of the "Triers" in 1654. He died in November 1655 and was buried in [Westminster Abbey](/wiki/Westminster_Abbey "Westminster Abbey"), but his body was exhumed and maltreated at the [Restoration](/wiki/English_Restoration "English Restoration").
